title: Life Science — Cells to Organisms
description: Explore levels of biological organization from cells to ecosystems.
objectives: Describe levels of organization: cell → tissue → organ → system → organism
Explain how cell specialization enables multicellular life
Compare unicellular and multicellular organisms

lessons.title: Levels of Organization
lessons.content: In multicellular organisms, cells specialize and work together.
examples: Muscle cells → muscle tissue → muscular system → organism
Unicellular: does all life functions in one cell (amoeba, bacteria)
Multicellular: division of labor — cells specialize for efficiency

lessons.title: Cell Division
lessons.content: Cells reproduce by dividing to allow growth and repair.
examples: Mitosis: produces 2 identical daughter cells (growth, repair)
Meiosis: produces 4 genetically unique cells (reproduction)
Uncontrolled cell division = cancer

title: Ecosystems — Cycling of Matter
description: Study how matter cycles through ecosystems via biogeochemical cycles.
objectives: Trace carbon through the carbon cycle
Describe the nitrogen cycle
Explain how matter cycling differs from energy flow

lessons.title: Carbon Cycle
lessons.content: Carbon cycles between the atmosphere, organisms, and Earth's crust.
examples: Photosynthesis: CO₂ → organic carbon (in plants)
Respiration and decomposition: organic carbon → CO₂
Fossil fuels: ancient carbon released back to atmosphere by burning — disrupts the cycle

lessons.title: Nitrogen Cycle
lessons.content: Nitrogen makes up 78% of air but most organisms can't use it directly.
examples: Nitrogen fixation: bacteria convert N₂ to ammonia (NH₃)
Nitrification: bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates
Denitrification: bacteria return N₂ to atmosphere

title: Chemical Reactions
description: Understand chemical reactions, balancing equations, and reaction types.
objectives: Recognize evidence of chemical reactions
Balance simple chemical equations
Identify synthesis, decomposition, and combustion reactions

lessons.title: Chemical Equations
lessons.content: Chemical equations show reactants → products, with atoms balanced on both sides.
examples: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (synthesis)
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (decomposition)
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (combustion)

lessons.title: Balancing Equations
lessons.content: Matter is conserved — atoms must balance on both sides.
examples: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (unbalanced) → 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (balanced)
Count each element on both sides; add coefficients to balance

title: Forces and Newton's Laws
description: Apply Newton's three laws to real-world situations involving motion and forces.
objectives: Apply Newton's three laws to scenarios
Calculate net force, acceleration, and momentum
Explain friction, gravity, and air resistance

lessons.title: Newton's Three Laws
lessons.content: Newton's laws govern all motion we observe in everyday life.
examples: 1st Law: A soccer ball stays put until kicked; a sliding puck keeps sliding until friction stops it
2nd Law: F=ma. A 10 kg object accelerated at 3 m/s² requires 30 N
3rd Law: Rocket propulsion; walking (push ground back, ground pushes you forward)

lessons.title: Friction and Momentum
lessons.content: Friction opposes motion; momentum is mass × velocity.
examples: p = mv: a 60 kg person running at 5 m/s has momentum = 300 kg·m/s
Impulse (force × time) changes momentum: airbags increase collision time to reduce force

title: Electricity and Circuits
description: Understand electric charge, current, and how circuits work.
objectives: Explain static electricity and charge transfer
Describe current, voltage, and resistance (Ohm's Law)
Analyze series and parallel circuits

lessons.title: Static Electricity
lessons.content: Charge builds up when electrons transfer between objects.
examples: Rubbing a balloon: electrons transfer to balloon (negative charge)
Opposite charges attract; like charges repel
Lightning: charge buildup between clouds and ground discharges dramatically

lessons.title: Circuits and Ohm's Law
lessons.content: V = IR: voltage = current × resistance.
examples: V=12V, R=4Ω → I=3A
Series circuit: one path; one bulb out = all out
Parallel circuit: multiple paths; one bulb out = others stay on

title: Astronomy — Stars and Galaxies
description: Study the life cycle of stars, types of galaxies, and the scale of the universe.
objectives: Describe the stellar life cycle
Classify stars using the H-R Diagram
Describe the structure of galaxies and the universe

lessons.title: Stellar Life Cycle
lessons.content: Stars are born from nebulae and end in dramatically different ways depending on mass.
examples: Low-mass star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
High-mass star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
Our sun is a middle-aged, medium-mass star ~halfway through its 10-billion-year life

lessons.title: Galaxies
lessons.content: Galaxies are vast systems of stars, gas, and dark matter.
examples: Milky Way: ~200-400 billion stars; barred spiral galaxy; ~100,000 light-years across
Three types: spiral, elliptical, irregular
Observable universe: ~2 trillion galaxies

title: Climate Change Science
description: Deepen understanding of the scientific mechanisms and evidence for climate change.
objectives: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect
Analyze climate data and trends
Evaluate mitigation and adaptation strategies

lessons.title: Enhanced Greenhouse Effect
lessons.content: Human CO₂ emissions are intensifying the natural greenhouse effect.
examples: Pre-industrial CO₂: ~280 ppm; today: ~420 ppm — highest in 800,000 years
Feedback loops: warming → melting ice → less reflection → more warming
Ocean acidification: CO₂ dissolves in seawater → carbonic acid → threatens marine life

lessons.title: Mitigation and Adaptation
lessons.content: Both reducing emissions and adapting to changes are necessary.
examples: Mitigation: renewable energy, electric vehicles, reforestation, carbon capture
Adaptation: sea walls, drought-resistant crops, early warning systems
Net-zero: balancing emissions with carbon removal

title: Biotechnology and Genetics
description: Explore modern genetic technologies and their scientific, ethical, and social dimensions.
objectives: Explain how DNA is used in biotechnology
Describe CRISPR gene editing
Evaluate ethical issues in biotechnology

lessons.title: DNA Technology
lessons.content: Scientists can now read, copy, and edit DNA.
examples: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): rapidly copies DNA — used in COVID tests, forensics
DNA sequencing: reading the order of base pairs — cost dropped from billions to ~$100
GMOs: organisms with modified DNA for desired traits (Bt corn, golden rice)

lessons.title: CRISPR
lessons.content: CRISPR-Cas9 allows precise gene editing.
examples: Can insert, delete, or modify specific genes
Medical potential: curing sickle cell disease, potentially preventing hereditary cancers
Ethical concerns: 'designer babies', germline editing, inequality in access

title: Earth History and Geologic Time
description: Read the fossil record and understand geologic time scales.
objectives: Describe methods of dating rocks and fossils
Explain major events in Earth's history
Interpret a geologic time scale

lessons.title: Dating Rocks and Fossils
lessons.content: Scientists use relative and absolute dating to determine ages.
examples: Relative dating: Law of Superposition — older layers are on the bottom
Absolute dating: radioactive decay — half-life allows calculation of age
Carbon-14: effective for up to ~50,000 years; uranium-lead: billions of years

lessons.title: Geologic Time
lessons.content: Earth is ~4.6 billion years old; life has been evolving for ~3.8 billion years.
examples: Hadean (4.6–4.0 Ga): Earth forms; molten, no atmosphere
Archean (4.0–2.5 Ga): first life (single-celled)
Cambrian explosion (~541 Ma): sudden diversification of multicellular life
Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction (66 Ma): asteroid wipes out non-avian dinosaurs

title: Physics — Energy, Work, and Machines
description: Understand work, power, simple machines, and mechanical advantage.
objectives: Calculate work and power
Identify six types of simple machines
Calculate mechanical advantage

lessons.title: Work and Power
lessons.content: Work = Force × Distance; Power = Work / Time.
examples: Lifting a 20 N box 3 m: W = 60 J
Doing 300 J of work in 10 seconds: P = 30 W
No movement = no work (in physics), even if you're pushing hard!

lessons.title: Simple Machines
lessons.content: Simple machines multiply force or change its direction.
examples: Lever: crowbar (MA = load arm ÷ effort arm)
Pulley: flagpole, crane (each additional pulley reduces force needed)
Inclined plane: ramp (longer ramp = less force but more distance)
Wheel/axle, wedge, screw are the other three
